title: Right Hand Limit
notes: **Definition.** lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = L means f(x) → L as x approaches a from the right, i.e. through values x > a; it is also written f(a + 0) or RHL.
**Substitution trick.** Put x = a + h with h > 0 and h → 0; then lim(x→a⁺) f(x) becomes lim(h→0⁺) f(a + h), which is usually easier to simplify.
**Worked example.** lim(x→0⁺) |x|/x = lim(x→0⁺) x/x = 1, because |x| = x for every positive x.
**Sign functions.** For f(x) = [x] (greatest integer), lim(x→2⁺) [x] = 2 while lim(x→2⁻) [x] = 1, so the two-sided limit at 2 does not exist.
**Vertical asymptotes.** lim(x→0⁺) 1/x = +∞; an infinite one-sided limit is still a valid description of behaviour but is not a finite limit.
**Exam caution.** Keep the strict inequality x > a throughout; including x = a or using negative h silently converts the RHL into a different question.
summary: The right-hand limit approaches a through values greater than a; substituting x = a + h with h → 0⁺ turns it into a one-variable limit.
